en: Vajra said:
The god Viṣṇu, the wide-striding one, is exceedingly easy to propitiate with a gracious countenance;
when praised, he revealed his universal form to the twice-born.
Speak of his supreme grace toward me, his devotee;
O Brahmin, I do not reach satiety while hearing this nectar of a story.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O great king, Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra, is an expert in ritual procedure;
he has a daughter who is his equal, renowned as Guṇakāśī.
In former times, Mātali and Nārada, while wandering through that entire forest, searched for the grandson of the merchant.
Having seized the nāga named Sumukha, the two of them departed;
then, from Śakra, they both requested him for that nāga.
Śakra granted a boon to both Sumukha and Tārkṣya, granting fearlessness from Tārkṣya to the former;
knowing the prowess of Tārkṣya, he [Sumukha] went into the presence of Keśava.
The slayer of Madhu granted Sumukha freedom from fear;
thereupon Tārkṣya, filled with wrath, approached Keśava.
Garuḍa said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, why do you bestow this boon upon Sumukha while disregarding me? Standing upon my back, you slay the enemies; do you not realize this?"
You protect me from an enemy who is a serpent, yet is the very one who devours my family.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus by him, Viṣṇu then spoke to Garuḍa.
[Viṣṇu:
"O Lord of Birds, I am not capable of bearing this entire world;
I alone support myself by means of my own self in every battle."
"If you have the strength to carry it, bear one of my arms.
Having said this, Hari placed his left arm upon his back.
Then, with a dejected countenance due to the loss of his wings, the best of birds,
exhausted and miserable, offered praise to Madhusūdana, the Lord of Gods.
Garuḍa said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who are worshipped by both gods and asuras;
O invincible one, lotus-eyed one, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!
My own strength was not recognized by me, for my mind was filled with self-conceit;
yet you alone, O sinless Lord, always sustain the three worlds.
O God, you alone always carry yourself by means of yourself;
for within your body, O God, the entire three worlds abide.
"How could even thousands of those like me possibly carry it?
Therefore, O Blessed One, be gracious toward me, who dwell under its banner."
O Lord of Gods, there is no end to your deeds within the three worlds;
who is capable of recounting your actions in their entirety?
Or what praise could there be for you, O Supreme Lord, beyond the mere recitation of your deeds?
You are omnipotent everywhere; be gracious to me, O slayer of my enemies!
O Vāsudeva, abode of all beings, Lord of the universe!
O Nārāyaṇa of great splendor, who reclines upon the ocean at the end of the aeon! Vdha_3,343.19 //
O you whose body is turned tawny by the filaments of the navel-lotus, be gracious to me; salutations to you, the one who dwells upon the bird-emblem on your banner.
The Blessed One said: "O Tārkṣya, you should never indulge in self-conceit;
I alone carry myself by my own power, and I sustain you as well."
Your wife was not pleased by you because you were rendered wingless;
for my entire three worlds have been placed upon my arm for your sake.
Indeed, there is no one else in the world as powerful as you;
for by the touch of your staff-like arms, no life has ever departed.
O best of birds, by whose power you have become strong and will undoubtedly possess extraordinary strength at the end of the fortnight.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed, Suparṇa again attained the state of having beautiful wings;
or rather, he obtained an increase in splendor and strength through the grace of the god.
Thus, O Tārkṣya, being praised like Puruṣa for the sake of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
you were once again made a Suparṇa and endowed with exceeding strength.
Merely by being asked by Śakra, even Sumukha was made an immortal;
therefore, O King, know this regarding that enemy of the Dānavas.
For there is certainly nothing that cannot be given to one's devotees, even the sovereignty of the gods;
likewise, for those seized by the noose of death, there is the falling into hell.
As soon as he was remembered, that Lord of Gods turned back out of fear of him.
May Madhuripu— the destroyer of enemies, who has eliminated all suffering for men devoted to him, who is worthy of worship by the best of the twice-born and the gods,
who moves like the king of birds (Garuḍa), and whose color is born of heroism— be pleased with you as you bow in devotion.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Sumukha," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. 3.343.
Vajra said:
"I wish to hear from you about that supreme grace which has been bestowed by the powerful Viṣṇu upon his devotee."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, when the three worlds had been slain by Bali in the past,
Śakra then went for refuge to his father Kaśyapa.
Then Kaśyapa, taking Śakra with him, went to the Grandfather;
Brahmā, the giver of boons, said to him: "Go, Kaśyapa, to Keśava."
Seek refuge with the god Madhusūdana, who reclines upon the ocean of milk;
entreat him for the status of a son, and he shall become your son.
"Then he shall give the entire triple world to the king of the gods. Thus addressed, Kaśyapa, together with the foremost of the thirty [gods], [acted accordingly].
Then, having gone to the Ocean of Milk, he beheld Hari through his ascetic penance;
having seen him, he praised him with a hymn, and then Hari [appeared] to him.
The Lord, the sustainer of the universe, being pleased, assumed the form of a dwarf and became my son; having traversed all the three worlds with those three strides, he pervaded them.
O Indra among kings, having bound Bali, the lord of the Daityas, he gave him over to Śakra;
and being thus praised by Kaśyapa, he attained the status of his son.
Vajra said:
"Recite that auspicious hymn which Kaśyapa used to praise Madhusūdana— a hymn that removes all sins."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, to the meritorious hymn proclaimed by Kaśyapa after he beheld the God of gods arisen from his bed upon the Ocean of Milk.
Kaśyapa said:
"Oṃ, salutations be unto you, O God of gods, O One-Horned One!"
O Vṛṣārcita,
O Sindhu-vṛkṣa, O Vṛṣākapi!
O blameless and auspicious one among the gods.
O Kapila, Viṣvaksena, Dhruva!
O Dharma, O Banner of Dharma,
O Vaikuṇṭha!
O Vṛṣāvarta,
you who are without beginning, middle, or end, beloved of the world.
O eternal one, born of the Vṛṣṇis, who lies upon the immortal.
O Three-abodes One, O Tuṣita of the three abodes!
O Dundubhi, you who are the great world and the navel of the worlds!
O Padmanābha, Viriñca, Bahurūpa!
O Agni, consumer of oblations, who are beyond destruction and free from the unfavorable states; O you whose axe is broken!
O Cakra, O Muṇḍakeśa, O Haṃsa!
O Hṛṣīkeśa, you who possess great liberality and subtle nature.
O Great Sage,
free from passion and darkness,
the foundation of all worlds!
O Śipiviṣṭa,
O sinless one, O first-born!
Born of Dharma,
whose navel is Dharma, whose navel is radiance.
O Candraratha, you alone are free from evil.
O ocean-dweller, unborn,
one-footed,
you who are manifested by a thousand.
O Great-Headed One, thousand-eyed,
thousand-footed!
O iron-faced Great Being,
thousand-armed one!
O thousand-formed one, thousand-eyed one,
source of a thousandfold manifestations!
Those who know the Vedas call you a knower of the Vedas by the thousands; they say that you alone possess the universal nature of all things, O Puṣpahāsa.
The supreme state of movement itself is *vauṣaṭ*,
*vaṣaṭ*,
and *svāhā*; it is the partaker of the portions in sacrifices, possessing a hundred streams and a thousand streams.
Whether it be *bhūḥ* or *bhuvaḥ*, you alone, O Brahmin, are composed of the Brahman.
You alone are Brahmā, you are the quarters, and you are the sky.
You are the earth;
you are Mātariśvan; you are the Hotṛ, the Potṛ, the thinker, and the leader.

You alone are the foremost cause of the oblation; you alone are the quarters of space by virtue of being the abode of the universe; you are the sacrificial vessel, the garland, and the one worthy of worship.
You have established [the path];
you alone are the refuge for those possessed of wisdom.
You are yoga, you are liberation, you are the supreme.
You are the ladle; you are the Ordainer; you are the sacrifice.
You are Soma,
you are smoke, you are consecration.
You are the sacrificial fee;
you are the universe; you are the steadfast.
O Turāṣāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, Nārāyaṇa!
O you who are like infinite light,
whose color is like that of the sun.
O Ādityatejas,
Great Being, Supreme Person!
O primordial deity, Padmanābha,
you whose smile is like a lotus!
O you who recline upon a lotus, whose eyes are like lotuses, and whose hair-tips are golden!
O pure one,
whose self is the universe,
O universal deity!
O you who have faces in every direction,
whose name is the universe,
and from whom the universe arises!
You alone are Viśvabhuj, the one who transcends the worlds through your stride, the maker of light, Śambhu, the self-born of the earth, the source of all beings,
and the Great Element.
Pervading all,
you alone are the protector of the universe.
You are the purifier,
the oblation that sustains all.
The upward action is the fall from the ground toward the summit of immortality.
O Agni, anointed with ghee,
O Brahmā of infinite deeds!
O Vaśapragya,
O Viśvapārśva, O Pārśva!
"O Viśvavara, you alone protect those who seek [your grace]"—
with this hymn composed by Kāśyapa, he who always performs the praise of the best of gods at dawn with a pure mind and thoughts fixed upon him shall go to the worlds of the Supreme Person.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn to Kaśyapa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said: "Tell me, who am a devotee, of that supreme grace of the high-souled Keśava, the god of gods, the wielder of the discus."
For I am never satiated by hearing that nectar of his ears,
he who alone in this world provides a protection for the hands of men falling [into distress].
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O sinless one, in ancient times the gods and the sages were disputing whether one should sacrifice with seeds that have been stored for up to three years.
"O knower of dharma, you ought to kill the goat for the sake of seeds that are unborn; this was the position held by the sages of purified souls."
But the bird of the gods, having then arrived by way of the path,
became the king named Uparicara, a Vasu and the best among those who possess the earth.
Then the gods and the sages questioned Vasu regarding how one should sacrifice with the materials as they had been previously described by Vasu.
Indeed, by means of that speech of falsehood which incited violence, the king,
having constantly become a sky-walker, came to dwell in a cavity within the earth.
Then the Dānavas, who were proponents of the cause of the gods, set their minds upon the destruction of Bhūmivivaraga, the devotee of the gods.
Having heard of their intended action, the gods of swift prowess reported it accordingly to Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods.
Then Bṛhaspati, having gone there, taught the king the invincible Vaiṣṇava protection within the cavity of the earth.

This lore (*vidyā*), which causes the destruction of all obstacles, was fashioned by Brahmā through the recitation of deeds past, present, and future; and having taught it to that king, Bṛhaspati said this to him:
Bṛhaspati said:
"O King, staying here you shall enjoy the stream of wealth offered by the twice-born;
through the grace of the deities, you shall be perpetually nourished by it."
"O King, by means of this knowledge,
you shall become invulnerable even while dwelling within a cavity of the earth against Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
Having spoken thus to the king, he vanished right there.
Vajra said:
"O best of the twice-born, tell me that protection which was performed by the priest of the gods;
for that protection of King Vasu while he was dwelling within the earth is considered by me to be supreme and foremost."

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Protection of Kings Residing in Subterranean Caverns," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva. Obeisance to Ananta.
To the thousand-headed one;
to him who reclines upon the ocean of milk;
to him whose couch is the coils of Śeṣa.
To the one whose vehicle is Garuḍa;
to the Unborn;
to the Unconquered.
O yellow-robed one!
O Vāsudeva!
O Saṃkarṣaṇa!
Pradyumna;
Aniruddha;
Hayaśiras.
Varāha; Narasiṃha; Vāmana.
Trivikrama / Rāma / Rāma / Rāma.
O Rāma!
Homage be unto you, homage be unto you, homage be unto you!

[Homage be unto you] against the Asuras, Varadas, Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Kumbhāṇḍas, Siddhas, Yoginīs, Ḍākinīs, and those headed by Skanda—the planets, the constellations, and other such malevolent spirits.
Destroy, destroy! Cook, cook! Grind, grind!
Destroy, destroy!
Put to flight, put to flight with the conch!
With the discus, the thunderbolt, and the mace.
Reduce them to ashes with the pestle and the plow! Vdha_3,346.0.[23]
O thousand-armed one!
O you whose weapons and arms are a thousandfold!
Victory, victory!
Victory, victory!
O Unconquered One!
O You of Unobstructed Vision!
Blaze, blaze!
Flare up, flare up!
O Viśvarūpa!
O Bahurūpa!
O Madhusūdana!
O Mahāvarāha!
O Great Being!
O Vaikuṇṭha!
O Nārāyaṇa!
Padmanābha;
Govinda;
Dāmodara.
O Hṛṣīkeśa!
O Keśava!
O Destroyer of all Asuras!
O benefactor of all beings! O shatterer of all evil dreams! O destroyer of all mechanical devices!
O crusher of all nāgas!
O great lord of all gods!
O liberator from all bonds!
O crusher of all that is harmful! O destroyer of all fevers! O warder-off of all planetary influences!
O pacifier of all sins!
O Janārdana!
Homage be to you, svāhā!

Whoever recites, reads, hears, remembers, retains, or proclaims this Aparājitā, the supreme Vaiṣṇavī, perfected Great Vidyā— for such a person there is no fear of fire, wind, thunderbolts, stones, or lightning, nor is there fear of the ocean.
There shall be no fear of planetary influences,
no fear of thieves,
nor any fear of wild beasts.

In some cases, there may be no night-time darkness, no women, no royal court, no hatred, no poison, no secondary poison, no toxic drug, no subjugation, no incantation for causing enmity, no incantation for driving away, no killing, no binding, or even no fear—
by means of these recited mantras, which are perfected, fully accomplished, and honored. That is to say:
Oṃ, salutations be to you,
O sinless one;
O unconquered one!
O Immeasurable One!
O Immortal One!
O Unconquered One!
O you who are perfected by recitation! O you who are perfected by remembrance!
O Ekānaṃśā!
Ume / Dhruve / Arundhati.
Sāvitrī; Gāyatrī;
Jātavedasī.
O Mānastoke!
O Sarasvatī!
O Dharaṇī!
Dhāraṇī; Saudāmanī; Aditi.
Diti,
Vinatā,
Gaurī.
Gāndhārī; Mātaṅgī; Kṛṣṇayaśodhā.
O speaker of truth!
O speaker of Brahman!
O Kālī!
Kāpāli / Nidre / Satyopayānakari / Vdha_3,346.0.[89]
Protect, protect from all beings and from all calamities, whether they be on land, in water, or in the atmosphere; *svāhā*!
If her flower withers away, or if her embryo falls out, if her children die, or if she becomes one who bears only a single child like a crow—*Vdha_3,346.1*.
Indeed, this [mantra] held as a weapon upon a wooden splinter in battle quickly destroys the pain of abdominal tumors, colic,
and eye diseases; it is the destroyer of headaches and fevers for all embodied beings.
Namely:
"Strike, strike! O Kāla! Move, move!"
O Gaurī, O Gaurī, blaze, blaze,
O Vidyā!
O you who are adorned with garlands, who possess fragrance, and who bind!
Cook, cook, O Vidyā!
Destroy, or rather, withdraw it; destroy the bad dream! Vdha_3,346.2.[1]
Nāśani / Rajani / Saṃdhye.
Dundubhināda, Mānasavega, Śaṅkhinī.
O Wielder of the Thunderbolt! O Wielder of the Discus! O Wielder of the Trident!
O destroyer of untimely death!
O Sovereign of the Universe!
O Drāvaḍi, Drāvaḍi!
O beloved of Keśava!
O accompanied by Paśupati!
O subduer of Dundubhi!
Śabarī;
Kirātī;
Mātaṅgī.
Oṃ drauṃ drauṃ jroṃ jroṃ kroṃ kroṃ turu turu, [subdue] all those who hate [me], whether openly or in secret.
Subdue, subdue! Crush, crush! Heat, heat!
Protect, protect!
Destroy, destroy!
O Brahmanas!
O Maheśvarī!
O Varāhī!
O Vaināyikī!
Upendri,
Āgneyi,
Cāmuṇḍe.
O Daughter of Varuṇa!
O Daughter of Vāyu!
Protect, protect!
O Pracaṇḍavidyā! Oṃ, sister of Indra and Upendra!
O Vijayā!
O you who increase peace, well-being, and nourishment;
O goad for desire;
O fulfiller of desires!
O bestower of the boon of all desires!
Make me beloved among all beings!
O attractor!
Āveśani!
Jvālāmālini!
Śoṣaṇi!
O Deluder!
O Blue Banner!
O Great Blue One!
Mahāgaurī / Mahāśrī / Mahācāndrī.
Mahāsauri; Mahāmāyuri; Ādityaraśmi.
O Jāhnavī!
O Yamaghaṇṭā!
Kiṇikiṇi!
Cintāmaṇi; Surabhi;
O you who have arisen from all the Asuras!
O you who milk all desires! May my purpose be accomplished according to my wish; svāhā!
Oṃ svāhā!
Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā. Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā. Oṃ svaḥ svāhā.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā! Wherever the sin has come from, let it go back there, svāhā! Oṃ bale!
O you of great power! O accomplisher of the unaccomplished! Svāhā! Om!
One should meditate upon the Vaiṣṇavī Aparājitā, which is unfailing and perfected through recitation.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Thus, for one who has performed the protection rite and partakes of the Vasudhārā [offering],"
The sons of Danu stood in the pit of Vasumatī while Vasu remained there.
Accompanied by fourfold armies and bearing various weapons, they arrived in diverse forms— burning with fierce speech and always cruel.
Having approached, they threatened Vasu with fierce words and struck him with terrifying weapons, being ever intent on the side of the gods.
They caused him no pain, nor did he even look at them;
instead, he meditated in his mind upon Madhusūdana, the Lord of Gods.
Then, seeing that great marvel, all those Daityas and Dānavas went home, dejected and their efforts rendered fruitless.
When those efforts proved fruitless, the Lord said to Garuḍa:
"O Garuḍa, go and quickly bring King Vasu here."
Thus addressed by the god of gods, the wielder of the discus, that Garuḍa departed, agitating the hosts of aquatic creatures as he stirred the ocean with the wind from his wings.
And he saw Garuḍa, the vehicle of Hari, in a pit of the earth with his eyes closed in meditation; even Vasurāja beheld him there.
Seeing that Garuḍa had arrived, endowed with devotion to Kṛṣṇa,
he of immeasurable deeds praised Garuḍa with words full of meaning.
Vasu said:
I bow to the mighty-armed lord of birds, whose vehicle is green,
who stands at the tip of Viṣṇu’s banner, and who terrifies the great asuras.
Salutations to you, O destroyer of the pride of the Nāgas, who increases the joy of Vinatā,
and who is gazed upon by the wretched Daityas as they are blown away by the wind from your own wings.
"O Supratīka and Vibhāvasu, by each other's curse,
you both have become an elephant and a tortoise, filled with mutual enmity."
The elephant is six yojanas in height and twice that in length;
the tortoise is three yojanas in height and ten yojanas in circumference.
O bird, those two were carried by you while remaining on your claws; they were killed and eaten, and having raised one another, they were both liberated from the door.
The cruel and blameless realm of the Niṣādas was enjoyed there;
then the lord of the Niṣādas was liberated by you, O Brāhmaṇa, even in that place.
By you, the branch of a *rohiṇī* tree, extending for a hundred *yojanas*,
was split apart where thousands of *vālakhilya* sages were staying.
Having placed them within his mouth by means of elephants and tortoises held by his claws,
he remained surrounded on all sides in the sky itself, which is without support.
O Kāśyapa, having conquered all the gods led by Śakra in battle, you brought back the supreme Soma from Agni.
Having made two serpents with poison in their gaze by means of dust upon his eyes,
he consumed those two created by the gods while they were constantly moving on the tips of his tongue.
"Even though you brought the Soma, it was merely carried away by you and not consumed;
for that reason, you have indeed become the mount upon the banner of Viṣṇu."
When you had placed the Soma upon the darbha grass, the Nāgas were deceived; for there, the slayer of Bala suddenly seized it. Act quickly!
O best of the twice-born, it was there that the tongues of the serpents were split in two,
and Vinatā was released from her slavery after having previously been defeated by Kaṭvā in a wager.
"Uccaiḥśravas is what color? "He is white," he said.
"I consider him black-haired, for I have seen his tail," [the other replied] through a play on words.
Formerly, for the sake of honoring Dadhīci, Vajra, and Śakra, you yourself, by means of a vajra-strike, [restored] that which was once possessed of wings; it was not otherwise.
When the Lord of the Gods could not find the end of that wing,
then your name "Suparṇa" became renowned throughout the three worlds.
O illustrious one, destroyer of the wings of the serpents, you are not equal to the god Bhāskara in splendor, nor to Samīraṇa in speed.
O All-pervading Lord, when you are merely absorbed in meditation, the entire universe of moving and unmoving beings,
as well as all fears, quickly come to destruction.
Carrying the entire universe with your own body and wings,
O Lord, you do not experience fatigue, just like the god Janārdana.
You are the seer, you are the highly fortunate one, you are the god, the lord of birds;
you are the sovereign, resplendent like the sun, and you are our unsurpassed protection.

Possessing the power of waves, virtuous, with undaunted spirit, prosperous, and difficult to overcome, you alone possess all asceticism and sacred learning; with unimpaired fame, you know the objects of the senses, both those yet to come and others.
You are the supreme; like the sun with its rays, you illuminate all this world of the moving and the unmoving.
Constantly eclipsing the splendor of the son of the Sun (Yama), you are the Ender of all this, both the permanent and the impermanent.
Just as the sun moves about consuming all creatures, so do you burn, O one with the splendor of fire;
terrifying like the fire risen at the end of an aeon, you bring destruction, O creator of the end through the turning of the serpent.
I have come for refuge to the Lord of Birds, who possesses great majesty and whose range is the cloudless sky;
having approached the mighty Garuḍa, the sky-ranger of great power, the granter of boons, invincible and tireless.
Thus ends the three hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Garuḍa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having been praised by the king, Garuḍa, though he had ascended his back,
revealed himself to the god Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor.
Having seen the Lord of the gods, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him,
he praised the unconquered Lord of gods with devotion, O king of kings.
Vasu said:
"Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, compassionate toward those who have come for refuge;
O destroyer of the pride of Daityas and Dānavas, the annihilator of the suffering of those who bow before you."
O granter of desires, O destroyer of desires, O source of the universe, O Lord of the world! You are the complete destroyer of the darkness that arises at night within the great form.
Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know your origin;
you are the beginning of all dharmas and of the seers, O Teacher of the World.
You are subtle, more vast than all beings great and small;
you are far-reaching, O illustrious one, and yet you have come to all.
Though dwelling within all beings, you are not smeared by their actions;
bodiless yet residing in bodies, you are established within all creatures.
You are the Puruṣa, you are the Unmanifest, and you are indeed the Self and the Intellect;
O Blessed One, you are likewise the great elements and the sense organs.
O Ancient One, knower of yoga, knowledge, and the object of knowledge, you are endured by yogis;
O Blessed One, those who worship you attain the supreme goal.

I have gone for refuge to Vāsudeva, the source of shelter, the victorious, the sinless, the unconquerable, the all-pervading God of gods, whose power is eternally intent on the destruction of the enemies of the thirty deities, who is worshipped by the twice-born and the best of gods, and who is the destroyer of all impurities.
Thus ends the three hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Hymn to Vāsudeva," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Viṣṇu, having been praised by Vasu, who was disguised as Vasu and was eloquent,
spoke to the king who stood before him with palms joined in reverence and body bowed low.
Vāsudeva said:
"O King, one must not speak a falsehood even when one's life-breaths are at the throat;
likewise, a question regarding dharma must not be addressed by one person alone."
O Knower of Dharma, even for one who is widely learned and desires the Dharma, these Dharmas are at times difficult to discern; O King, they are subtle and hard to follow.
Therefore, one who knows should never speak [falsely] alone;
by speaking a lie, O lord of men, you have incurred great hardship.
Likewise, the loss of my status was obtained by the astrologer who spoke the truth;
because you have been constantly devoted to me, I have granted you this remedy.
In a short time, by means of this ritual, that which cannot be achieved even by the gods and asuras—
go, protect the kingdom, and remain likewise unshakable.
You must never, under any circumstances, show contempt toward Brahmins;
for a Brahmin is to be known as a great being and the supreme deity.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus to Vasu, Viṣṇu vanished on that very spot, O King;
and accompanied by Tārkṣya, Vasu was filled with wonder.
He regained his kingdom once more, as well as the power of moving through the air;
thereafter, he was honored by all the gods who had assembled there.
Thus, that lord of the earth, dwelling in the subterranean realm (rasātala), was indeed filled with devotion by the god;
having been liberated from that most terrible fear and endowed with his kingdom, he likewise departed through the sky.
Thus ends the three hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Vasus," in the third section of the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. // 348 //
Vajra said:
"O enhancer of the Bhṛgu lineage, describe the universal form of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods; to whom was it shown by him?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The universal forms of the God, which were beheld many times in the past by those devoted through single-minded contemplation, are impossible to describe."
Without the grace of Vāsudeva, one would not possess divine vision;
indeed, the power to behold the one who bears the universal form does not exist [without it].
In that regard, O sinless one, I shall relate to you that which was previously shown to Nārada by Viṣṇu, the God of All.
Nārada went to that most enchanting Badarī-āśrama, a truly great sacred site dedicated to Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Therein Hari, who is fourfold in nature, attained the state of being the son of Dharma—
namely Hari Kṛṣṇa, Nara, and the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
At that time, Hari-Kṛṣṇa was indeed present in another world,
while the two gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa were likewise engaged in fierce ascetic penance.
They stand upon a beautiful, auspicious vehicle with eight wheels;
both have one leg, are without support, and likewise have both arms raised upward.
There Nārada beheld those two gods of blazing splendor; having offered his salutation, he stood before them as they departed.
Then, having been honored with water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and other rites, that twice-born one dwelt there in the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Once, while staying in his hermitage, that best of brahmins beheld those two most excellent gods, who were blameless, creating an obstacle to a divine rite.
Then, having performed their daily rites, Nārada spoke to those two teachers of the world:
"You two are the lords of the worlds; you two are the supreme sovereigns."
For whose propitiation here are you both engaged in this ascetic practice?
Who is being honored by you both, and who is provided for in the rites for the gods and the ancestors?
That which is our supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*), from which the origin of everything arises—
that unconquered one, [he manifested] as a new [form] for the purpose of demonstrating the bounds of cosmic order.
O Brahmin, we always worship the brāhmaṇas— the teachers of the gods— as well as the cows and the ancestors, in rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors throughout the three worlds.
Those who worship him, indeed worship that very God, the Supreme Lord;
whoever worships this deity, by him Hari is worshipped.
O highly fortunate one, even if performed without the prescribed rites, for He is omnipresent;
therefore, one who desires to perform the worship of another deity should instead worship Hari.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, his worship of the deity should be performed according to the prescribed rite;
for within that deity reside all the gods and even the entire three worlds.
The worship of Viṣṇu performed by one who follows the prescribed rites constitutes a worship of the three worlds;
for there is no such thing as Brahman in the worlds where Janārdana is not present.
There is nothing in the worlds that is not established in Viṣṇu;
in whom all is, from whom all is, who is all, and who is everywhere.
Salutation to that Self of All, who is eternally composed of everything.
In the midst of the Ocean of Milk, there is an island extending for many yojanas.
There those men were white, possessing a splendor equal to the moon,
and all were endowed with the marks characteristic of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Those who know the ritual procedures of the Pañcarātra always worship Hari;
even the Lord Madhusūdana, having assumed a body of māyā, worships him.
Hari always accepts their worship upon his head;
he constantly sports with them and is ever worshipped by them.
Those men here who have attained a state of single-minded devotion, and those who always worship the Lord of the World even without desire; Vdha_3,349.25 //
Abandoning their bodies, they go to that island known as Śveta;
free from outflows, without need for food, they are all-knowing and all-seeing.
All-powerful and eternally satisfied, having attained supreme bliss,
they worship Hari there for another hundred divine years.
Then, O Brahman, having pierced the solar orb, they enter Aniruddha by means of their austerities; thereafter, they enter Pradyumna and then the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Having then attained Vāsudeva, they all become equal to him; everywhere and at all times, they possess all powers.
"Released from all sufferings and having attained supreme bliss,
you must go quickly from here to those who dwell on Śvetadvīpa."
Behold, O Brahmin, that all-pervading Lord is pleased with you;
he will show you his form, which is most wonderful and marvelous to the three worlds.
O tiger among Brahmins, the entire universe was pleased with the slayer of Madhu,
as were Ekata, Dvita, and Trita, who possessed great ascetic power.
O Brahmin, although they went to that place, Janārdana was not seen by them,
because they had approached the Teacher of the World with single-minded devotion.
Only this verse was recited by those highly fortunate inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa, who were entirely free from all taints.
Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Being, Primordial One!
O highly fortunate one, having heard this verse and likewise the bodiless voice of Hari, which carries the words of the learned and sustains all beings, they were filled with wonder.
Having reached Śvetadvīpa, one never encounters death again;
O twice-born ones, there is no access to Śvetadvīpa except for those who are single-mindedly devoted.
You possess a general devotion and are rich in asceticism;
endowed with fierce austerity, you have therefore come to this region of mine.
And you who possess general devotion and goodness, go back without delay;
by you, O men, have the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa been seen.
By these verses, Janārdana is thus beheld by those men who are devoted to exclusive meditation; indeed, [he is seen] through these verses.
O Brahmins, you should constantly recite this; then you shall return here once more.
This verse is purifying, meritorious, and the destroyer of all sins.
The wise person should perform the recitation and the fire-oblation with devotion according to the verses;
likewise, the offering of incense, lamps, food, and flowers should be presented.
O Brahmins, one should recite this verse during prostrations and circumambulations;
likewise, O twice-born ones, one should perform the ritual bath with it and drink water at the conclusion.
This verse, which removes all sins, is meritorious, bestows liberation, grants all desires, and is auspicious; it has been declared as the provider of every wish.
One who has fallen into calamity should likewise recite it for the sake of liberation;
the wise person should perform its recitation constantly.
By the recitation of this, a person attains all desires;
having heard these words of yours, those Magadhas have indeed returned.
There they saw Vasu, the lord of the earth, performing a sacrifice,
for whom the righteous-souled Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, was the officiating priest.
The invisible portion there was taken by the god Viṣṇu;
all the deities took their shares from the visible portion of the priest.
Ekata, Dvita, and Trita spoke thus to Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, who had turned away his anger toward Viṣṇu.
"Invisible to all the gods, how can you wish to see him? Thus was Devācārya Bṛhaspati entreated.
Then the sages, having attained a state of single-minded devotion, brought that sacrifice of the king to completion and [honored] Janārdana.
O twice-born one, in former times I came from Śvetadvīpa for the sake of the gods' work;
now I have reached Śvetadvīpa once again, a place from which return is difficult to obtain.
Therefore, O Nārada, behold that Lord of the gods stationed there;
for you, too, must perform many tasks for the sake of the gods.
O twice-born one, even though you have gone to Śvetadvīpa, because of that [transgression],
you shall not now attain in the worlds that state which brings about liberation;
however, O brahmin, at the end of the kalpa, you will go to that destination.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus, Nārada then quickly saluted those two gods and departed for that island with a speed equal to that of the mind or the wind.
Having gone there, Nārada beheld the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa, and with devotion, he honored them by bowing his head.
Having reached the great White Island with a joyful mind, Nārada beheld those very same white men, auspicious and possessing the luster of the moon.
He worshipped them with his head and his mind; being thus honored by them, he was remembered as one intent on recitation, desiring to see [the goal], and enduring all hardships.
Becoming single-minded, the brahmin of mighty arms raised his arms aloft and sang a hymn of praise to the Universal One, who is beyond all qualities yet whose essence is the qualities.
To Vāsudeva, the peaceful one, likewise the creator of the universe, O twice-born;
to the infinite, the immeasurable, the all-pervading, and the one of supreme speed.
To that Viṣṇu of immeasurable strength and prowess, who is eternally worshipped by the gods and sages,
who destroys the burden of existence and rebirth, and who removes the sins of those who bow before him.

Thus ends the three hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn by Śrī Nārada in Śvetadvīpa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: He then beheld Viṣṇu, Hari, who bears the universal form, joined with colors resembling white, yellow, red, and black.
In some places joined with black, in some places colored by black;
in some places resembling the moon, and in some places like vermilion.
In some places it resembles emerald, in others it has the luster of a ruby;
in some places it is like gold, and in others it has the radiance of a blue lotus.
In some places it has the luster of *pāṭala* flowers, in others it resembles the sky; in some places it is like powdered saffron, and in others it resembles powdered turmeric.
In some places resembling dust or stone, in others like sapphire, and in various places bearing indescribable colors; thus it appeared in various ways here and there.
There were also many faces of various kinds of beings,
as well as those of Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Śakra, Yama, and Varuṇa.
Of Dhanada, Hutāśana, Vāyu, and Nirṛti;
likewise of the planets, the constellations, and the Rudras together with the Vasus.
O twice-born one, likewise for the Ādityas, the Maruts, and the Bhṛgus;
and similarly, O King, for the Aṅgirases together with the Sādhyas and the Aśvins.
Then [he was born] among the Daityas, the Nāgas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rakṣasas;
likewise among the Pitṛs, the Pannagas, the Yakṣas, and the Piśitāśins.
Of humans, horses, and elephants; of elephants, horses, deer, and birds; of leopards, tigers, and lions—indeed, of all living beings.
He beheld his faces by the hundreds and thousands— some gentle and some terrifying.
In the mouths of that fierce one, he saw numerous multitudes of living beings on all sides, as well as fires being swallowed by Viṣṇu.
Then Nārada beheld various mounts emerging from his gentle mouths, as well as the creatures issuing forth from them.
And hands of various forms, endowed with diverse mudrās,
joined with thousands of kinds of vessels and weapons.
Some [are adorned] with the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the sacrificial altar, the *camasa* cups, *kuśa* grass, the black antelope skin, and the sacred fires;
and some with the water-pot (*kalaśa*), the bell, the conch, the lotus, the blue lily, and so forth.
Some [are armed] with swords, clubs, discs, shields, spears, and axes;
others with nooses, great staffs, scimitars, arrows, and bows.
Some [carried] *bhuśuṇḍī* spears, clubs, javelins, thunderbolts, stones, and *paṭṭiśa* weapons; others carried citron fruits, rosaries, and full vessels.
Thus, the best of sages, possessed of great splendor, beheld his innumerable hands, each endowed with various kinds of vessels.
Furthermore, according to the rules prescribed in the treatises on dance,
he beheld the heads, eyes, and hands of that god during the performance of the dance.
And the Supreme Sage [perceived] the entire three worlds within his body,
including the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
The sage beheld the entire world— including the continents, the oceans, the worlds, and the nether regions— residing within the body of the God.
Having seen that supreme form, he was both terrified and thrilled with wonder;
with tears in his eyes, he fell at his feet, bowing his head.
And with that very hymn previously mentioned, he praised Janārdana;
thereupon the God, smiling, spoke to that best of sages.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Arise! Do not fear, O knower of dharma; choose a boon as you desire.
Śrī Nārada said:
O God, may there be constant and exclusive devotion toward you;
I desire no other boon than this, which is the highest for men.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the Lord Hari, who removes the distress of those who bow before him, spoke to him:
"This which you have seen of me is established in your very nature."
O Brahmin, this universe of manifold forms should likewise be disregarded by you; for the austerity you have practiced, O sage, is the same as that which I have practiced.
"O twice-born one, having assumed this form, my own form has been shown;
by my own will, I can assume forms by the hundreds and thousands."
O best of the twice-born, whatever forms belong to the gods and others in the three worlds, know them to be mine alone; there is nothing whatsoever other than me.
I am the past and the future, and likewise the present;
I am all that is stationary and all that moves, O Nārada.
Both the real and the unreal—I myself declare this truth to you here:
it is without sound, without taste, and devoid of touch, smell, and form.
Know me, O Nārada, as all-pervading in the ultimate sense;
whoever shall offer praise to me with this hymn composed by you, [shall attain his goal].
I shall provide him with all desires, both divine and human;
upon his death, he shall attain the destination of Śvetadvīpa.
"Even after reaching Śvetadvīpa, you shall remain healthy for as long as the duration of this Varāha-kalpa remains."
When the Vārāha Kalpa has passed, there will then follow the Mātsya Kalpa,
since very many tasks for the sake of the gods must be performed by you.
And having appeared, I am to be instructed by you in that manner;
O Brahmin, thousands of my manifestations have already passed away.
There will be others as well; listen to some of them from me:
"When the world has become a single ocean, I lie upon the couch of Śeṣa."
When the Grandfather (Brahmā) remains asleep with Lakṣmī as his companion,
I exist as a fish, likewise as a tortoise, and I am also a swan, O Nārada.
O Brahmin, by me in the form of a woman, the Daityas and Dānavas were deceived;
likewise, by me in the form of Hayagrīva, the Vedas were taken away from the Dānavas.
Having become a boar, I lifted up this earth;
as a boar, I slew the Daityas who dwelt in the depths of Pātāla.
Hiraṇyākṣa, who was fierce in his strength, was slain by the best of men in the form of a boar;
and the Dānavas were killed in battle by him whose essence is Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, on the supramundane path, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and I too— Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by me in the form of Narasiṃha.
O Brahmin, having become Vāmana in ancient times, I took away the three worlds from Bali with three strides, out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
"I am the Vāḍava fire dwelling in the ocean, and I always drink the water;
O Brahmin, the earth is Vasumatī, and it was made so by Pṛthu and by me."
By me, as Kapila, the wicked sons of Sagara were to be consumed by fire;
likewise, by Dattātreya, the earth, the gods, and the hosts of the twice-born were restored.
By Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, the earth was made light;
it had to be cleared twenty-one times, oppressed as it was by the burden of the Kṣatriyas.
And having bestowed the four sons upon Daśaratha and myself,
Rāma must carry out the slaying of Rāvaṇa for the happiness of the people.
Likewise, the destruction of Gandharva must be accomplished through the self of Bharata;
the slaying of Meghanāda must be performed by Lakṣmaṇa, and likewise by me.
Śatrughna must likewise carry out the slaying of Lavaṇa,
and I, Vālmīki, must compose the Rāmāyaṇa poem.
"The Vedas were to be spoken by Vyāsa, and the great narrative of the Mahābhārata was to be told by me,
O tiger among Brahmins, through my identity as Dvaipāyana."
Having attained the status of Pāṇḍu’s sons in five ways, and likewise in two ways through Vasudeva, I shall thus lighten the burden of the earth.
In the world of men, the Daityas who have taken human form must be slain;
and by me and Balabhadra, the Mauṣṭikas and others must be destroyed.
The mighty ones, headed by Kaṃsa, are to be slain by me, Kṛṣṇa;
and the mighty Śambara is to be slain by Pradyumna.
And hundreds of thousands of Daityas were to be slain by Aniruddha,
by Sāmba, by Yuyudhāna, and likewise by me as well.
Furthermore, as a Buddha, I must proclaim the Dharmas in the Kali Yuga;
likewise, by means of Viṣṇu’s power, the Mleccha kings must be slain.
Know that the universal monarchs on earth are born from a portion of me;
likewise, the sages are to be understood as having arisen from my very own portions.
Whatever being possesses majesty, splendor,
or power, know that to be born from but a portion of my radiance.
Or rather, O sinless one, what is the use of this extensive knowledge for you?
Having pervaded this entire universe, I remain established by a single fraction of myself.
Therefore go; O best of the twice-born, may you always possess mental perfection.
Upon reaching the end of the kalpa, you shall enter my body.
Having spoken these words, the venerable Nārada vanished on the spot; he then performed worship for the inhabitants of that region.
Honored by them, that brahmin, firm in his vows, bowed to them and then departed quickly for the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
There he fell at the feet of those two venerable sages;
honored by them, the brahmin then dwelt in that hermitage.
Then, on one occasion, those two whose wealth was penance said to that brahmin:
"We have seen you in the same way as Acyuta when he had gone to Śvetadvīpa."
O tiger among sages, having approached the God of gods at his ease within that body, there is no one more fortunate than you in this world.
O Brahmin, you have seen Hari, who assumes the universal form,
the essence of the three worlds, the Lord of the universe, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him.
Since this favor has been bestowed upon you by the divine Viṣṇu,
therefore learn this secret, the supreme procedure for his worship.
O best of Brahmins, this divine [mantra], which performs all rites, bestows all goals, and is auspicious, must not be given by you to one who is not a devotee.
Having worshipped Janārdana, who has attained a state of exclusive devotion, according to the prescribed ritual,
a man goes to that unsurpassed and auspicious island, from which, once gone, he does not return again.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Universal Form," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. 351.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa said:
"At the very outset, in any delightful location— whether near a lake, a river, a spring, a house, a grove, or a mountain peak—
one should prepare a level, charming mandala measuring one cubit."
Therein, in the center, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus;
then, one should divide it with the previously described square enclosure marked by four gates.
Then, one should meditate upon a white hundred-petalled lotus in the center of the pericarp of that lotus.
Upon its pericarp is a sun mandala;
above that, a moon mandala;
and above that, a fire mandala.
In the center of that, one should place the Supreme Person—bodiless, without smell, without taste, without form, without touch, without sound, all-pervading, the end of liberation, the syllable Om.
One should place the syllable *A*, Vāsudeva, upon the eastern petal of the lotus;
one should meditate upon him as being white in color.
One should place Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose form is the syllable *Ā*, on the right;
one should meditate upon him as having the luster of a lotus petal.
One should place the syllable Oṃ as Pradyumna on the western petal and meditate upon him as being yellow in color.
One should place the syllable *Aḥ*, representing Aniruddha, on the northern petal and meditate upon him as being black in color.
One should place Brahmā upon that petal in the northeast;
one should meditate upon him as having the luster of a lotus petal.
One should meditate upon him as equal to ten million suns.
One should place Varāha upon the petal in the northwest;
one should meditate upon him as being like crushed collyrium.
At the eastern gate, one should place these syllables— oṃ, keṃ, ṭeṃ, yeṃ— representing Vainateya,
and one should meditate upon him as being golden in color.
At the southern gate, one should place the Sudarśana discus, the chariot of splendor;
one should meditate upon it as having a diamond navel, a thousand spokes, and a radiance equal to ten million suns.
One should place the Śārṅga bow at the western gate;
one should meditate upon it as resembling Indra’s rainbow.
One should place Aniruddha at one's own spot on the northern door;
one should meditate upon him as being of all colors.
With the syllables *veṃ*, *ṇeṃ*, *kṣeṃ*, and *kṣeṃ*, one should place the Pāñcajanya conch in the intermediate directions;
one should meditate upon it as having the color of the moon.
One should place the syllables *dheṃ*, *heṃ*, *bheṃ*, *heṃ*, and the lotus of Śrī on the right;
one should meditate upon her as white.
One should place Puṣṭi within the lotus with the syllables *geṃ*, *ḍeṃ*, *veṃ*, and *śeṃ*,
and meditate upon her as white.
One should place the *vanamālā* (forest garland) in front with *heṃ seṃ*;
one should meditate upon it as being of many colors.
One should place Nandaka in the northeast of the city;
one should meditate upon him as having the color of the sky.
Saying "Oṃ," one should place the armor in the southeast and meditate upon it as having many colors.
Oṃ jheṃ leṃ: one should place the Śrīvatsa and meditate upon it as white.
Oṃ cheṃ ṭheṃ: one should place the Kaustubha gem in the northwest;
one should meditate upon the radiant Āditya.

Then, one should place the lords of the directions— Śakra and Agni, Yama and Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Pavana, Kubera, and [the lord] in the northeast— in their respective positions on the outer part of the maṇḍala;
one should meditate upon them in the forms as previously described.

With the twelve-syllable mantra ending in "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya," one should offer the guest-water (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), unguents, flowers, lamps, incense, honey-mixture (madhuparka), food offerings (naivedya), fruits, and edible snacks to the Puruṣa in the center of the pericarp.
Or with the mantra "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya," or else with the eight-syllable mantra:
"Oṃ, victory be yours, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
May your mind be gracious, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Being, Primordial One."
With this mantra, or with the Puruṣasūkta,
he should then worship the other deities seated upon the petals individually, each with their respective mantras as previously described.
The man who worships Viṣṇu according to this procedure shall accomplish all his goals and indeed becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Having created a disease, he devours the afflicted; he does not do it, nor does he incur that [sin]. But this other [act] is auspicious, glorious, meritorious, purifying, and a destroyer of evil.

Health, the increase of wealth and grain, the destruction of enemies, and subjugation— whatever man constantly worships the God according to this rite, he produces prosperity; or, if that does not please him, then having reached Śvetadvīpa and pierced the solar orb, he restrains [the senses], attains Pradyumna and Saṃkarṣaṇa, and having attained the state of a noble deity, he reaches the state of being partless (niṣkala).

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Method for Worshipping Nārāyaṇa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard this which was uttered by Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Nārada [praised] Madhusūdana constantly according to this very procedure.
The righteous-souled one worshipped him with his inner self absorbed in that;
then the Blessed One [performed] the *puṃsavana* rite for the high-souled Nārada.
Then, perceiving Nārada directly before him, he spoke these words:
"Go, O auspicious Nārada; wander through the worlds as you desire."
I shall grant you a vision at whatever time you desire,
having obtained this favor from the Lord of Gods, Puruṣottama.
Nārada wandered through the worlds, constantly worshipping Hari;
this universal form was seen by the high-souled Nārada.
Furthermore, by that very same high-souled Prahlāda, who had assumed the form of a man-lion, and likewise by him when his body was filled with nectar.
In ancient times, it was beheld by Brahmā during his conquest of the three worlds;
furthermore, it was seen by the ten-necked Rākṣasa on the western ocean.
In the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, when the enemy of Madhu had gone as a messenger,
he was examined by the sages in the midst of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s assembly.
Likewise, Arjuna beheld it during the Mahābhārata war,
when he was agitated by the fear of losing his kinsmen and was awakened by it.
When the Bhārata war had ended, as they were returning to Dvārakā,
that was seen by the high-souled Uttaṅka who had encountered them on the way.
Govinda, the Lord of the three worlds, who is ever affectionate toward his devotees—
he who constantly proclaims his deeds, that man [attains the highest state].
Or, O protector of the earth, one who hears this with purity and a mind focused upon it shall be liberated from all sins and go to the supreme goal.
Thus, O King, that foremost of the best of the twice-born obtained grace from the boon-granting god;
indeed, through the grace of King Bhaktikramakraiyan, men obtain their desires from him.
Thus ends the three hundred fifty-third chapter, titled "The Grace of Nārada," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
